episodes.168149: During the early morning hours of May 30th, a few discrete/semi-discrete supercells developed across central MN producing low-end severe hail. However, the main focus of the event was a QLCS moving northeast from FSD���s CWA into south-central to central Minnesota. After crossing into the MPX CWA in southwest Minnesota, this feature transitioned to more of a line/bow echo but no damaging wind reports were observed, likely due to the large amount of MLCIN in southern Minnesota. However, lesser MLCIN and slightly better low-level lapse rates across central MN allowed for the bow echo's  winds to start reaching the surface with an 84 mph wind gust measured at the Olivia AWOS. A grain bin was blown away near Sacred Heart as well as some trees and power lines downed near Belgrade.
episodes.168150: A strong synoptic cyclone swinging into the Northern Plains set the stage for a late Spring severe weather outbreak on May 30th. Discrete and semi-discrete supercells developed during the afternoon ahead of an arcing cold front and a nearby surface low. These storms quickly traveled northeast while gradually growing upscale into bowing line segments as storms merged together and new cells formed. During this time, hail and tornadoes occurred; the strongest being an EF2 through Forada, MN. The bowing line segments became dominant and a wind event unfolded.||Strong and broad synoptic lift, little capping, and questionable mid-level shear likely allowed for upscale growth. This caused storm interactions and competing updrafts which may have limited mesocyclone longevity and strength. While property was damaged, no lives were lost on the last day of a holiday weekend when many people were outdoors camping or doing other recreational activities.

episodes.168677: A surge of deep tropical moisture from the northwest Caribbean Sea as high pressure built across the western north Atlantic resulted in numerous showers and scattered thunderstorms.  Several areas of gale-force wind gusts developed from thunderstorm outflows.
episodes.168687: Strong to severe thunderstorms impacted a large portion of the Sandhills and north central Nebraska during the evening, overnight into the morning hours of May 29-30th. Thunderstorms initiated over the northwestern Sandhills and tracked east across the area. The thunderstorms were in association with an approaching cold front and strong upper level disturbance. Hail up to six inches in diameter and thunderstorm wind gusts up to 60 MPH were reported with the strongest storms.
episodes.168727: Storms redeveloped in the late morning, with supercell characteristics across eastern South Dakota producing up to one inch diameter hail and winds of 70 mph, in addition to 6 confirmed tornadoes, one of which was rated EF3. Heavy rain also occurred with this system, with the greatest amount of rainfall measured by a CoCoRaHS observer being 4.69 inches measured near Columbia, and the highest COOP observer report coming out of Milbank with a two day total of 2.86. This heavy rain resulted in flooding in several rural locations but also included parts of Watertown and Aberdeen.
episodes.169150: Precipitable water values were only around an inch with dry mid levels. Moisture slowly increased in the afternoon with sea breeze initiated strong to pulse severe storms in the late afternoon and evening along mergers.
episodes.169156: An upper level low along the coast of southeast Georgia moved slowly inland through the day. The 12Z JAX sounding showed steep low/mid lapse rates and cool temperatures aloft. MUCAPE was also over 3000 J/kg. Winds throughout the column were relatively light , and sea breeze boundaries moved inland along both coasts. Scattered thunderstorm developed along the sea breeze boundaries with a merger near the I-75 corridor in the late afternoon where a few strong to severe storms formed.
episodes.169217: Thunderstorms moved through central and south central Kansas during the evening into the overnight hours. These storms produced quarter sized hail and 60 to 70 mph winds. Heavy rainfall associated with the storms led to flash flooding as well in central Kansas.
episodes.169261: An enhanced risk for severe weather resulted in a few damaging wind gusts, 1 inch hail reports, and an EF-1 tornado.
episodes.169273: Iowa was placed within the warm sector of a strong surface low pressure system, and the tight pressure gradient and deep mixing allowed for gusty south winds. A handful of station even gusted over 50 kts with some damage reported. Meanwhile, a dryline initiated convection across parts of northern Iowa in the late afternoon and evening. These storm primarily produced strong winds, though quarter sized hail was reported by one observer. Later that night, the cold front brought through another round of non-severe thunderstorms.
episodes.169359: A summer pattern was in place with a moist and unstable airmass in the afternoon.  As a result, few strong to severe storms affected the area with impacts to trees and powerlines across portions of Jefferson and Madison counties.
episodes.169366: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed in a moist and unstable airmass with reports of severe weather in Lowndes county.
episodes.169403: A cluster of thunderstorms came up through south central South Dakota in the evening and overnight hours, and proceeded northeast across central and eastern South Dakota with multiple reports of 1 inch hail and wind gusts of 60 mph.
episodes.169404: Supercell storms in northeast South Dakota moved into west central Minnesota during the mid-day hours, producing an EF1 tornado by Artichoke Lake, ping pong sized hail in rural Traverse county and winds of 60 mph near Graceville. Heavy rain was also associated with the system with COOP observers measuring 3.78 inches in Wheaton and 2.42 inches in Browns Valley. The heavy rain associated with this system produced flooding in rural areas of Big Stone and Traverse counties.
episodes.169405: Afternoon storms caused by an upper-level disturbance produced nickel sized hail and a thunderstorm wind gust of 69 MPH. The storms began forming in Colorado and traveled northeast through Northwest Kansas and Southwest Nebraska.  Meanwhile high winds occurred behind a boundary that was behind a cold front.
episodes.169428: Afternoon storms caused by an upper-level disturbance produced gusts up to 59 mph from decaying storms. The storms began forming in Colorado and traveled northeast through northwest Kansas and southwest Nebraska.
episodes.169431: Line of strong to severe thunderstorms brings isolated large hail and damaging winds to portions of south central Nebraska during the late evening of May 29th. Overall, the primary severe weather focus on this date was focused further north, across north central and northeast Nebraska. However, a southwest to northeast oriented line of thunderstorms developed from Dawson County northeast to Valley and Greeley Counties between 11PM and midnight CDT and became marginally severe. Large hail nickel to quarter size was the primary threat, but isolated wind damage to a few power lines and poles in Valley County was also noted. After midnight, the line began to shift northeast and affect mainly areas of Valley, Sherman, and Greeley Counties. Severe thunderstorm warnings, and even a couple of tornado warnings prompted by low to mid level rotation on radar, continued until 1:30AM CDT on the 30th, but no additional severe reports were received.
episodes.169432: Strong storm system brings severe thunderstorm and non-thunderstorm wind gusts to portions of south central Nebraska during the daytime hours of May 30th. An intense mid and upper level storm system, by late spring standards, shifted across the central and northern Plains and brought a few rounds of thunderstorms through the area. Severe thunderstorms occurred the night before over northern portions of the forecast area, and there was a several hour lull before a new line of thunderstorms developed in roughly the same area during the late morning hours. Isolated sub-severe hail was reported with this line north and northeast of Grand Island between 11AM and noon CDT before this line also shifted northeast out of the area.||Strong surface low pressure associated with the deep upper trough moved south-southwest to north-northeast across the forecast area during the late morning and early afternoon hours. The attendant dry line rapidly surged through the area and brought strong south to southwest winds. Most wind gusts were around 45-50 MPH, but a 58 MPH gust was observed at Central Nebraska Regional Airport in Grand Island. Damage was also reported in Polk County where medium sized tree branches were downed and fencing was damaged. This dryline swept much of the low to mid level moisture out of the area for several hours. However, wrap around moisture arrived from the west and northwest and allowed for new showers and thunderstorms to move through the area between 2PM and 5PM. Much of this convection was rather weak and high based, but it was strong enough to mix already strong ambient winds down to the ground. A couple 60 MPH wind gusts were measured in Dawson and Sherman Counties, and a 67 MPH gust was measured in Greeley County. No particularly serious damage was reported.
episodes.169450: Two reports of Quarter sized hail. The storms that caused this hail formed in the wake of other storms that produced an orphaned outflow boundary earlier in the evening. Weak cells of storms began forming in eastern Colorado but they quickly intensified as they crossed into southwest Nebraska.

episodes.169844: Supercells developed along a front and produced hail, strong winds and some flash flooding during the afternoon and evening of 5/30.

episodes.170023: A strong area of low pressure across the Northern Plains lifted a warm front across the Northland on Memorial Day morning. Showers and storms moved through during the morning hours with the atmosphere recovering during the afternoon hours. A few of the storms were severe during the morning and produced small hail and tree damage. An arc of thunderstorms developed across southwestern Minnesota and adjacent areas of Nebraska, South Dakota and Iowa by the mid-afternoon hours and moved to the northeast and across the Northland for the late afternoon and evening hours. These storms were much stronger and contained very strong winds that produced widespread damage across the region. Additionally, there were a few embedded tornadoes with the storms with the strongest tornadoes producing EF-1 damage in the Deer River and Hinckley areas.
episodes.170064: A strong area of low pressure across the Northern Plains lifted a warm front across the Northland on Memorial Day morning. The hail was around 1 inch in diameter.

episodes.170290: An amplified and vigorous upper level pattern pushed several weak disturbances northeast across the region during the overnight and early morning of May 30th.  With ample elevated instability on the order of 2000-2500 J/kg available and effective shear of 35 to 45 knots, storms became severe across south central South Dakota and north central Nebraska and organized into a large scale QLCS as it moved east and northeast into Minnesota and Iowa late night. Several QLCS tornadoes developed from the Sioux Falls area eastward.  Widespread winds of 60 to 90 mph caused scattered tree damage, with isolated pockets of more significant structural damage. Presidential Disaster Declarations were granted to Lyon, Rock, and Nobles Counties in Minnesota for damages to public infrastructure.

episodes.170395: There was barely a break between the exit of the earlier morning severe convection, and development of the next round during the later morning and early afternoon on May 30th across southeast South Dakota.  A series of impulses moved northeast during the day, with a leading strong wave moving out of Nebraska by early afternoon. Storms blossomed near a cold frontal boundary toward the James River Valley, despite the limited diurnal destabilization, due to steep mid-level lapse rates which brought MLCAPE up to 1500-2000J/kg in the warm sector. Strong mid-level winds led to long, linear hodographs. With a warm front also lingering north of Interstate 90, storms that interacted with enhanced low-level shear in the vicinity of various boundaries produced a few brief tornadoes, but strong forcing eventually resulted in an evolution toward linear structures with mainly damaging wind.  Near the core of the upper level wave, a secondary band of thunderstorms developed across Nebraska during the late afternoon and raced northeastward through early evening, featuring mainly damaging wind gusts. Some enhanced non-thunderstorm wind gusts occurred with initial showers in the lower Missouri River Valley in the late afternoon.

The first indications of tornado damage were just east of Interstate 29 near 186th Street. A farm had mangled tree branches through the tops of the shelter belt, a destroyed outbuilding, a west facing garage door and garage rafters bowed in and three pickups with the back windows broken out. The track continued a quarter mile to the north, where a second farm had uprooted trees, complete destruction of a machine shed and a collapsed barn. The main residence also had loss of shingles and the loss of a small portion of roof panels. The track continued northeast. The next residence to sustain damage was near 772nd Ave and 181st St. The tornado entered the farm from the west where it uprooted several trees and broke branches off the tops of others, a third of a roughly 300 foot long milk barn was leveled, one stave silo completely collapsed and a second was razed about half way to the base. Further east on the property a shelter belt was managed and an empty grain bin was tossed east northeast about a quarter mile into the neighboring field. An outbuilding south of the property also collapsed. Just shy of a mile to the northeast along 473rd Ave a machine shed buckled on the southwest side. Another quarter mile to the northeast another farm sustained significant damage. On this farm a tornado path was noted through the trees on the west side of house. Trees were uprooted and one tree twisted counter clockwise. On the main residence eight sheets of plywood were ripped off the roof and insulation was blown out of the attic. Roof material was found in trees and debris spread 200 or 300 yards to the north northeast. Residents were in the basement at the time and noticed that their ears popped. They also noted that water was drained from toilets and plumbing traps after the storm. Power lines were downed near 474th Ave. Another several miles to the northeast, near 179th Street and 475th Ave, another farm sustained significant damage. On the south side of the property several pieces of farm equipment were moved, tipped or tossed and a grain bin was dented. Trees were uprooted south of the house and the house sustained window damage. Walls collapsed on both a barn and machine shed on the property. Another smaller shed was also destroyed. A path of debris was noted about a quarter mile northeast of the property. The last property damaged by the tornado was located at 177th Street and US Highway 15. This property had tree damage and lost a shed.
A large tree was taken down by thunderstorm winds.
Thunderstorm winds flipped a camper on Interstate 29 north of exit 121.
Crop damage is an estimate from insured losses. Information provided by the United States Department of Agriculture.
Occasional quarter to ping-pong ball size hail was reported.

A grain bin in a field near 496th Ave and 179th Street was ripped from the base and tossed a mile to the northeast. Roughly three and a half miles northeast on 176th St a farmstead lost several outbuildings and had roof and window damage to the home. Another two miles to the northeast three metal truss transmission towers were damaged, one completely twisted and collapsed. The strongest winds were confined to the area of the transmission towers. Roughly three and a half miles northeast, just north of US Highway 212, a shed was destroyed and a path was noted through a shelterbelt. The very last indications of the tornado was north of 169th Street on 476th Ave where the path was noted through a shelter belt.
Fallen trees and limbs resulted in a power outage along E Ash St.
A clear path was observed through a tree grove. Additionally, farm machinery was tossed around on the property.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 63 mph was measured by South Dakota State University mesonet site SFSS2 in Sioux Falls.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 64 mph was measured by South Dakota State University mesonet site OAKS2 4 miles south-southeast of Astoria.
Heavy rainfall resulted in water flowing outside a shallow creek bed. This water approached homes.

Two properties near the intersection of 164th St and 475th Ave sustained damage. The first farm had a roof ripped off a barn, damage to a machine shed, a destroyed stave silo, debris pierced through house walls, roof panels off house, broken house windows, snapped and uprooted trees, and a dented grain bin. The second residence had half a barn roof ripped off and tossed a quarter mile to the northeast. The track continued northeast roughly six miles, crossing Grant County Highway 15, between 158th St and 159th St. Near this location a farmstead sustained complete loss of a machine shed and power lines were downed. The track would come to an end roughly two more miles to the northeast near 157th St, where another farm would sustain complete loss to a machine shed and debris spread across the field to the north northeast.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 70 mph was measured by a hand-held anemometer near Brandon.
Wind estimated at 70 mph brought down three large spruce trees, and a large limb fell onto a vehicle. Some light farm equipment was knocked over, and a steel garden shed was blown into the street.

The south to north tornado track started south of 156th St along 482nd Ave where a farm exhibited clear tornado damage which included mangled trees, barn roof damage, barn doors split in half, residential roof and siding damage and a camper completely destroyed. The track would continue roughly three miles north in the vicinity of 153rd St. Another farm would sustain damage, with tops of trees missing in one shelterbelt and uprooted and snapped trees in a second shelterbelt. The dormer of the residence was ripped off and landed 85 to 100 yards from the house in a northeast direction. North of this property a dairy farm had a machine shed with collapsed walls. This farm was housing dairy cattle that were transported from the Estelline area after a May 12 tornado destroyed barns on that property. The last indication of the tornado track was through a shelter belt a quarter mile north of 153rd St.
ASOS site KRSW Southwest Florida International Airport reported a 63 mph wind gust.

Lightning struck the roof of a home in the 22600 block of SW 109 Court in Princeton. A patch of about 75-100 barrel tiles at the tip of the roof were broken off by the lightning strike. A fire was sparked but was put out by firefighters before any additional damage could occur.

A tornado briefly spun up in open fields and lowlands around 3 miles north-northeast of Sherman.  The tornado was viewed moving northeast and soon dissipated. The tornado caused no damage from which the NWS could assign an EF-scale rating. The average path width was estimated at 20 yards.
Station at McCook Airport. Wind gust from decaying thunderstorms.
Severe winds downed multiple trees and blew over a shed.
A video showed a brief tornado spinning up in open farmland. The tornado caused no damage from which the NWS could assign an EF-scale rating.  The average path width was estimated at 20 yards.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 60 mph was measured by Minnesota Road Weather Information System site MN027 1 mile west-northwest of Lake Benton.
Numerous small tree limbs were downed by thunderstorm winds.
Crop damage is an estimate from insured losses. Information provided by the United States Department of Agriculture.
A tree was blown down and blocked Thompson Valley Road between Highway 19 and Curtis Mills Road.
Several grain bins and sheds were badly damaged. Numerous trees were broken. Shingles were removed from a house.

A storm chaser documented the brief tornado touchdown. Two farmsteads were damaged. The first farm was located near 410th St and 590th Ave. This farm exhibited a clear track through trees on the property, the house had shingle damage and damage occurred to small outbuildings. Roughly three quarters of a mile to the north, near 400th St, the second property was damaged. This property had a grain bin swept off the base, complete destruction of machine shed, shingle damage to the home and a clear path of mangled trees.
A survey team viewed the damage in Appleton but was unable to determine whether it was due to a downburst or tornado. Several dozen trees were broken.

A brief tornado developed about 3 miles north northwest of Milan. It uprooted several trees and then moved into Swift County where it significantly damaged farm outbuildings. Maximum winds for the Chippewa County portion were estimated at 70 mph.

A tornado developed about 3 miles north-northwest of Milan in Chippewa County and then moved into Swift County where it uprooted a number of trees and significantly damaged farm outbuildings. Maximum winds for the Swift County portion were estimated at 90 mph.

This tornado developed about 5 miles southwest of Danvers and tracked north until an outflow boundary caught up with it, then the tornado tracked northeast to 7 miles northwest of Clontarf.  It originated in Swift County, then moved through the southeast corner of Stevens County, then into Pope County, where it dissipated. Several wooden poles with electrical transmission lines were snapped. Irrigation systems were overturned, trees were damaged, and some structural damage to homes and farm outbuildings also resulted. Maximum winds were estimated at 100 mph.
Fallen trees or limbs resulted in a power outage off of Waukeenah Highway.
A tree was blown down and blocked the westbound lane of Highway 90 near Rainey Run.
A tree was blown down near Old Lloyd Road and Gamble Road.
Fallen trees or limbs resulted in a power outage along Willie Road.
A wind gust of 60 MPH was measured by a mesonet station located one mile southwest of Eddyville.
The tornado hit several farms.  It broke some windows, knocked down or broke dozens of trees, tore tin off several sheds, and caused major damage to barns.  Maximum winds were estimated at 90 mph.
Several trees were blown down north of Chokio.
Multiple small tree limbs were downed by thunderstorm winds.

This tornado developed in Swift County, about 5 miles southwest of Danvers and tracked north until an outflow boundary caught up with it, then the tornado tracked northeast to 7 miles northwest of Clontarf. It moved through the southeast corner of Stevens County, then into Pope County, where it dissipated. Several wooden poles with electrical transmission lines were snapped. Irrigation systems were overturned, trees were damaged, and some structural damage to homes and farm outbuildings also resulted. Maximum winds were estimated at 100 mph.
Utilities reported a loss of $30,000 due to downed power poles.
A farm shed was destroyed.

This tornado developed in Swift County, about 5 miles southwest of Danvers, and tracked north until an outflow boundary caught up with it, then the tornado tracked northeast to 7 miles northwest of Clontarf. It then moved through the southeast corner of Stevens County and into Pope County, where it dissipated. Several wooden poles with electrical transmission lines were snapped. Irrigation systems were overturned, trees were damaged, and some structural damage to homes and farm outbuildings also resulted. Maximum winds were estimated at 100 mph.
A large spruce tree was blown down near Donnelly.
Tornado spun up just west of Lake Emily and tracked northeast. Some trees were snapped and farm outbuildings were damaged. Maximum winds were estimated at 95 mph. This tornado was filmed on video.
A wind gust of 60 MPH was measured by a mesonet station located four miles west-southwest of Hazard.
Numerous large cottonwood, ash, and spruce trees snapped or uprooted around Niemacki Lake Park. Wind gusts from 60 to 80 mph affected much of Macsville Township 411 pm CDT.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 63 mph was measured at Automated Weather Observing System site KMML near Marshall.
Numerous small tree limbs were downed by thunderstorm winds.

A tornado developed about 4 miles west of Starbuck and tracked northeast. A small outbuilding was completely destroyed and debris was spread north northwest. A truck and trailer were overturned on Highway 28. Maximum winds were estimated at 90 mph.
Spruce trees uprooted and large ash tree limbs broken in southwest Western Township. Time estimated based on radar.

This tornado was wrapped in damaging downburst winds and rain as it rapidly tracked northeast for roughly 6 miles to around 3 SE of Elbow Lake by 419 pm CDT. Numerous wooden single and double X-Braced power poles were snapped, including a nearly 2-mile stretch of double pole structures along 240th street, as a broader downburst wind pattern developed. Numerous trees of all kinds were snapped or uprooted. Several farm buildings and grain bins were destroyed. Max winds to 120 mph, Max width to 350 yards.
Quarter to half-dollar size hail fell for a few minutes.

This tornado was wrapped in damaging downburst winds and rain as it rapidly tracked to the northeast for about 11 miles, ending around 4.3 miles NNE of Elbow Lake by 424 pm CDT. Numerous ash, spruce, cottonwood, and willow trees were snapped or uprooted. Numerous wooden power poles were snapped Numerous farm outbuilding and steel grain bins were destroyed, with roofing and wall panels carried downwind for a mile or more. Max winds were 115 mph, with a max width to 400 yards.
Large trees were blown down, and a shed was destroyed.
Several power poles were bent or snapped.

Numerous large ash and spruce trees snapped or uprooted around town. One of 4 large 100k bushel steel grain bins was blown down at the Elbow Lake cooperative grain elevator. Wind gusts likely ranged from 70 to 90 mph for several seconds. Time estimated based on radar. The Elbow Lake wind sensor went offline due to widespread power outages.
There were parts of a grain bin that blew across railroad tracks near Hanley Falls.

Numerous large ash and spruce trees snapped or uprooted at the Tipsinah Mounds Campground. Damaging downburst winds impacted much of Erdahl Township with wind  gusts from 70 to 90 mph. Two storage building were blown down near the Tipsinah Mounds Golf Course. Report augmented by NWS damage survey. Time estimated based on radar.

A semi tractor-trailer combination traveling on westbound I-94 was blown over onto an SUV that had parked on the shoulder of the highway due to an approaching storm. Reports indicate that three individuals were transported to a local hospital with non-life threatening injuries. Time estimated based on radar.

A tornado originated on the east side of Lake Reno in Pope County. At first, it damaged about a dozen trees, but quickly became more intense and broke or uprooted several hundred trees before entering Douglas County. Maximum winds for the Pope County portion were estimated at 105 mph.
A transmission line was blown down south of Hazel Run.
Large branches broken down and trees uprooted near downtown Ashby. Wind gusts estimated from 70 to 80 mph.
Several trees and power lines were blown down near Wegdahl.

A detached garage was destroyed, house roofing torn off, trees snapped, and a center pivot irrigation system flipped over along or near the south shore of Ten Mile Lake. Numerous large ash and spruce trees were also snapped or uprooted on east and northeast edges of the lake, and across much of Tumuli and St. Olaf Townships. Information augmented by NWS Storm Damage Survey. Winds gusts estimated from 70 to 90 mph. Time estimated based on radar.

A tornado entered Douglas County from Pope County, just east of Lake Reno. It immediately demolished a garage and broke many hundreds of trees before hitting an area of homes along the east side of Maple Lake in the city of Forada. Dozens of homes had roofs torn off, garages and sheds destroyed. It threw a car several hundred feet. The tornado tore part of the roof off from the fire station. It continued beyond Forada and hit numerous farmsteads before hitting the west side of the city of Nelson, where a farm lost most outbuildings and a home lost its roof. The tornado continued moving northeast, hitting more farms, before dissipating several miles east of Carlos. Maximum winds were estimated to be 120 mph.
Several trees and power lines were blown down around the city of Granite Falls.
Large trees were blown down from about 3 miles west of Dalton, through town, and to points east and northeast of town. Winds gusts estimated from 70 to 80 mph. Time estimated based on radar.

A fifth wheel dual-axle camper was flipped over near Stalker Lake. Numerous large trees were snapped or uprooted around Stalker and Long Lakes. One pole shed had its south facing wall blown inward and sheet metal panels blown off. Information augmented by NWS Damage Survey. Winds gusts estimated from 70 to 90 mph. Time estimated based on radar.
Several 4 to 8 inch diameter branches were broken down in farmstead shelter belts across Oscar Township. Time estimated based on radar.

This tornado was wrapped in damaging downburst winds and rain as it rapidly tracked to the north northeast. Numerous poplar, ash, and spruce trees were snapped or uprooted. Shingles and metal roofing panels were torn off of houses and farm buildings and were spread downwind. Peak wind estimated to 90 mph. Time estimated based on radar.
Wind-driven dime size hail caused some damage to vegetation.
A few 6 to 8 inch diameter branches were downed by thunderstorm winds, as well as a  15 inch limb which blocked a city street.
Thunderstorm winds dislodged locked machine shed doors.
Large trees were blown down near Inspiration Peak.
Large trees were blown down and a travel trailer was crushed by falling trees on South Turtle Lake. Time estimated based on radar.
Peak wind measured at a personal weather station near South Turtle Lake before the station lost power.
Trees blown down, house and shed roofing torn off, and a pontoon boat flipped near Wall Lake. Winds gusts estimated from 70 to 80 mph. Time estimated based on radar.
A wind gust of 67 MPH was measured by a mesonet station located seven miles north-northeast of Wolbach.
Peak wind measured at a personal weather station.
Peak wind measured at a personal weather station. A few 8 inch diameter pine trees were snapped along CR1, southeast of Phelps.
Five power poles were snapped or cracked in Amor Township. Time estimated based on radar.
Trees blown down on a pickup truck. Time estimated based on radar.
Cattle barns a complete loss. Delayed report, time estimated from radar.
Tree down across road near intersection of Poplar St & Wild Turkey Trail.
Numerous tree limbs were downed by thunderstorm winds.

This tornado was wrapped in damaging downburst winds and rain as it rapidly tracked to the north northeast, into and across Big Pine Lake. Numerous poplar, ash, spruce, and pine trees were snapped or uprooted. One garage had an overhead door blown in and the back wall blown out, though the roof remained intact. Peak wind estimated to 100 mph. Time estimated based on radar.
Report of numerous trees down with structural damage near the intersection of Mt Paran Church Rd and Brown Hill Church Rd.
A few poplar trees were blown over.

This tornado tore through the eastern side of Eagle Bend. It knocked down or snapped many trees, partially removed roofs from several houses, peeled tin off the roof of multiple sheds and buildings, and took the top off three massive and filled grain bins in Eagle Bend. Multiple farmsteads were hit, destroying barns, machine sheds, and other outbuildings. It ended about 5 miles west-southwest of Staples where the scattered tree damage pattern could no longer be determined to be of tornadic origin. Determination of the specific path was assisted by Todd County Emergency Management, which provided drone imagery to the NWS. Maximum winds were estimated to be 100 mph.
Personal weather station measured a peak wind gust of 65 mph.
Report of tree down across road near the intersection GA-83 and Moina Michael Rd.
A few 8 inch diameter poplar trees were snapped throughout central Leaf Township. Time estimated based on radar.
A few 8 inch diameter poplar trees were snapped throughout central Leaf Township. Time estimated based on radar.
A few 8 inch diameter poplar trees were snapped throughout central Leaf Township. Time estimated based on radar.

Metal roofing and side panels were blown off a pole-shed with metal sheets strewn about and wrapped around trees near the intersection of State Highway 87 and CR43. Numerous poplar trees were snapped or uprooted across Spruce Grove and Runeberg Townships. Time estimated based on radar and public reports.
Several large tree limbs, and power lines were blown down, including a piece of sheet metal on power lines.
Metal roofing was peeled off of a garage. Time estimated based on radar.
Report of tree down on powerlines near intersection of Pleasant Valley Rd NE and Mount Paran Church Rd.
Multiple trees blown down. Some trees have fallen on power lines. Shingles were torn of the roof of a house.
Several poplar and ash trees were snapped across western Blueberry Township. Time estimated based on radar.

A tornado developed in far northern Todd County and hit two farmsteads before exiting into Wadena County (see corresponding entry from NWS Grand Forks). At the first farmstead, a garage door was blown in and part of the garage roof came off. Maximum winds for the Todd County portion were estimated to be 90 mph.
Quarter sized hail and winds gusting to 70 mph, about 3 W of the Staples Airport.

This tornado was wrapped in damaging downburst winds and rain as it rapidly tracked to the north northeast from the Todd County line, across far southeast Wadena County for about 9.5 miles, to the Cass County line. It snapped numerous single pole and double X-braced power poles. it tumbled at least three center pivot irrigation systems.  Numerous oak, ash, and pine trees were snapped. The Old Wadena and Bullard Campgrounds had swaths of pine trees laid down. One cabin had the roof and sidewalls torn out. Peak winds to 130 mph. Time estimated based on radar.
Numerous trees blown down.
A trained spotter estimated a wind gust of 60 mph.
Public reported a large tree branch down via social media.
Several trees were blown down near Sleepy Eye.

This tornado was wrapped in damaging downburst winds and rain as it rapidly tracked to the northeast from about 2 NW of the Staples Airport to about 2 NNE of the Staples Airport. It appears to have developed roughly half a mile east of an earlier tornado, based on divergent tree damage paths and supported by radar depictions. It snapped several poplar, ash, and spruce trees along its path. Peak winds to 90 mph. Time estimated based on radar.
Large trees blown down. Time estimated based on radar.
FL Highway Patrol reported a tree blown down across the southbound lane on County Road 137 near State Road 247.

The tornado crossed into Cass County from Wadena County along County Road 30 just south of 84th Street Southwest and tracked northeast for about half a mile before lifting just after crossing 84th Street Southwest. The tornado blew a center pivot irrigation system across 84th Street Southwest, snapping power poles in the process. No other damage was observed. The time of the tornado was estimated by radar and peak winds were around 100 mph.

Peak wind measured at the Park Rapids Airport, KPKD. Numerous pine and poplar trees were snapped or uprooted across Todd and Arago Townships, from Fish Hook Lake northward through Potato, Eagle, Island, and Cedar Lakes. Time ranged between 529 and 539 pm CDT based on radar, nearby wind sensors, and public reports.
Several trees were blown down in St. James, including some that landed on homes and damaged them.
Norfolk ASOS measured a peak wind gust of 58 mph.
Several poplar. pine, and ash trees were snapped or uprooted across Two Inlets and Savannah Townships. Time estimated based on radar.

A tornado caused damage in southwest Cass County, mainly across Poplar Township. The tornado began near the Poplar Cemetery and tracked north-northeast. Around a dozen power poles were snapped near the base along 60th St SW to the west of Highway 64 along with numerous tree damage, including several very healthy pine trees with trunks 12-18 inches in diameter snapped at the base. A small piece of farm equipment was also tossed roughly 100 yards. Significant tree damage was observed along Highway 64 around the intersection of 56 St SW, with damage continuing to the northeast into a wetland/bog-type landscape that was inaccessible. Peak winds were estimated to be 105 mph.
Large poplar and pine trees snapped or uprooted across Lake Emma and Clay Townships.  Time estimated based on radar.
Several trees were blown down in Fairfax.
Another burst of an estimated 60 mph winds occurred. There were some downed tree limbs as well.
A few trees were down across Minnesota Highway 210.
The FL Highway Patrol reported a tree blown down across Highway 129 near 254th Terrace.
Several trees and power lines blew down, some landed on homes and damaged their roofs around New Ulm.

Several large pine, ash, and poplar trees were snapped or uprooted across Clover and Lake Alice Townships. One or more snapped trees were evident along Highway 71 every 100 yards or less through these two townships. Power was lost to the MnDOT RWIS station along Hwy 71, between Douglas Lodge and Lake George. Time estimated based on radar.
An estimated gust of 60 mph occurred with a downed tree limb. The report was received via Twitter.
Several pine and poplar trees snapped or uprooted across Hendrickson and Lake George Townships. Time estimated based on radar and nearby wind sensor reports.
Several pine and poplar trees were snapped or uprooted along CR2, from southeast Bear Creek Township into eastern Itasca Township. Time estimated based on radar and nearby wind sensor reports.
Large trees blown down. Time estimated based on radar.
Multiple trees were down onto power lines and buildings. One tree had an estimated diameter of 12 to 14 inches based on a photo that was received.
Shed, barn and tree damage was noted on a social media posted in the city of Winthrop.
Public report of quarter sized hail.
Photos were received showing several trees down with tree debris scattered over the road.
Extensive damage was reported to several farms and homes in the area.
The local emergency manage indicated that numerous trees were blown down or uprooted between Winthrop and Gaylord.
A cluster of trees was down onto a power line on County Highway 11.
Multiple trees were down in the Pine River area.
Large trees blown down along U.S. Highway 2.
A few trees were blown down with numerous branches down as well.
Multiple trees were down and the power was out.
A tree was down on a vehicle.
Thunderstorm winds removed a few shingles from a house.

A thunderstorm wind gust of 61 mph was measured by South Dakota State University mesonet site CTNS2 2 miles east-southeast of Colton. Crop damage is an estimate from insured losses. Information provided by the United States Department of Agriculture.
Photos were received showing large trees snapped at the base with several down on power lines.
Several trees were uprooted or snapped in New Auburn.
Quarter sized hail reported.
A boat lift and a dock were flipped on Lower Whitefish Lake.
Several large tree branches were blown down around Hutchinson.
Large trees blown down.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 65 mph was measured by South Dakota Road Weather Information System site SD520 3 miles west of Dell Rapids.

Numerous trees and uprooted or broken. Several farms were hit, with machine sheds and other outbuildings collapsed or losing roofs. The tornado then crossed into Carver County (see corresponding entry).
Photos were received from the Chippewa National Forest of numerous small to medium trees down over forest roads.
A photo was received showing a 12 to 14 inch tree that had been snapped.
Highway patrol reported a semi-trailer flipped one mile north of Dell Rapids.
Several large pine trees were uprooted and knocked over.
A pine tree estimated to be 12 to 14 inches in diameter was down on a deck.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 60 mph was measured by Automated Weather Observing System site KMDS 1 mile northeast of Madison.
Report from mping.
A few large trees were down in the area.
Thunderstorm winds flipped over a dock on Little Boy Lake.
A large limb of an oak tree about halfway up was broken off. Numerous small branches were also blown down along with several nearby small trees.
A large shed was damaged, including a tree that blew down on a vehicle south of Dassel.

This tornado formed in McLeod County (see corresponding entry) before entering Carver County. It then uprooted or broke dozens of trees. The tornado also caused significant damage to a machine shed. The tornado then moved into Wright County (see corresponding entry).
Several trees and large branches were downed, including some on power lines.
A photo was received of an estimated 10 to 12 inch diameter pine tree down.
Several trees were blown down around Cokato.
Roof damage in Mayer was noted on a social media post.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 69 mph was measured by Automated Weather Observing System site K4P3 3 miles east of Egan.
Several trees were blown down around Howard Lake.
Several trees and power lines were downed, with one partially blocking a road.
After moving in from Carver County, the tornado dissipated shortly after entering Wright County, but it still caused large limbs to be broken on about one dozen trees.
Several large branches were downed, some of which were partially blocking a road.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 70 mph was measured by South Dakota State University mesonet site FLNS2 3 miles north-northeast of Flandreau.
Several trees and power lines were blown down near Hahira.
Several trees were also reported down in Pierz.
Numerous trees were blown down near Delano.
A few trees were blown down in Waverly.
Numerous trees were blown down northeast of Montrose.
The emergency manager estimated a gust to 60 mph.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 68 mph was measured by South Dakota Road Weather Information System site SD577 13 miles west of Ward.
Two trees were downed and a chicken run, cow shed and grill were all lost or damaged along with lots of debris blown around as well.
Several pine trees were uprooted between Maple Lake and Monticello.
In addition to the hail, there were 60 to 70 mph winds that occurred. This did result in downed tree limbs.
Law enforcement reported 60 to 70 mph winds and quarter sized hail.
Several large pine and poplar trees were snapped or uprooted along Highway 72, between Shooks and Kelliher. Time estimated based on radar and nearby wind sensor reports.
Report was received via mPING.

A damage survey team viewed damage north of Buffalo but it was inconclusive whether the damage was due to a downburst or tornado. Several trees were uprooted or broken, a garage door was dented in, shingles were partially removed from a house, and an irrigation pivot was tipped over.

A brief tornado started near the intersection of County Road 63 and Becker road. The tornado tracked north-northeast, sporadically knocking down trees along the way. While the tree damage was not as significant as other storms on this day, drone imagery provided by a spotter depicted a very clearly convergent signature in the tree damage. The most significant damage from this tornado was the partial lifting off of a roof from a two story home, though no broken windows were noted and |otherwise shingle damage appeared very minor. Sporadic tree damage continued in a path to the north towards the Mississippi River where the damage path appeared to end. Peak winds were estimated to be 85 mph.
A few large tree limbs were blown down near St. Michael.

A tornado produced a path of damage through the city of Deer River, with damage to numerous homes and businesses. The tornado likely began somewhere just south of Highway 2, though a precise location was difficult to determine due to a lack of |damage. The first damage observed was a camper/RV that was in a parking lot south of Highway 2 which was tossed across the highway into the parking lot of a furniture store building just north of the highway. The furniture store building had all of its south |facing windows blown out with damage to the front facade and some evidence of roof lift on the flat portion of the roof. The building also lost part of a gabled metal roof. A metal shed/outbuilding in the parking lot was completely destroyed. To the north, a two story building that includes a funeral home and post office had evidence of roof lift. Continuing north through the residential streets numerous trees were downed and several outbuildings - sheds and garage buildings - sustained significant damage, with some collapsing and others sliding off their foundations. This damage continued north- northwest, crossing state highway 6 around 7th Ave. Damage to the ball fields north of|town are believed to be part of the tornado���s path, with a small outbuilding and dugouts being destroyed and damage sustained to the metal chain link fence. Tree damage continued onto private property to the northwest, with the end of the tornado path estimated to be near or just south of County Road 142. Peak winds were estimated to be 107 mph.
A garage was collapsed by the winds with debris strewn about in Deer River.
Several trees approximately 8 to 10 inches in diameter were blown over. A large tree around 18 to 24 inches in diameter was also blown down about 1 mile to the northwest of the report location.
Several 8 to 10 inch diameter trees were uprooted or snapped.
A photo was received showing a 6 to 8 inch diameter tree down along with snapped limbs.
A large tree blew down in Big Lake.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 68 mph was measured by Minnesota Road Weather Information System site MN029 5 miles south of Hendricks.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 70 mph was measured at mesonet site AT653, 3 miles west of Arco.
Two 8 inch pine trees were downed by the storm.
A few moderate-sized tree limbs were downed by thunderstorm winds.
A mobile mesonet station measured a 62 mph wind gust. Crop damage is an estimate from insured losses. Information provided by the United States Department of Agriculture.
A wind gust of 64 mph was measured by a personal weather station.
At least 5 balsam trees were down with all falling to the northwest. Numerous conifer branches and tops were also down as well.
A few trees and power lines were blown down in Elk River.
Several large pine and poplar trees were snapped or uprooted along Highway 72, near Waskish. Time estimated based on radar and the power outage at the Waskish Airport weather station.
WeatherFlow site XSKY Skyway Fishing Pier reported a 60 mph wind gust.
